What is unemployment?

ECON 104
04

Who is unemployed?

To be considered “unemployed,” you have to meet four conditions:

  1. You are 16+ years old
  2. You are not institutionalized (not in prison)
  3. You do not have a job
  4. You are actively looking for a job
The fourth point is crucial. If you’re not looking for work, you’re not considered unemployed.
ECON 104
05

Who is not unemployed?

  • A 6-year-old
  • A retired 60-year-old
  • Someone who has become a stay at home dad and has given up looking for a job
ECON 104
06

The Labor Force

It is all the adults (16+) capable of working and either looking for work or currently working.

It consists of both:

  1. The employed: individuals aged 16 and older who have a job
  2. The unemployed: individuals aged 16 and older who are jobless, and have actively looked for work in the prior four weeks, and are currently available for work.

How good an indicator is the unemployment rate?

  • Doesn’t measure the quality of jobs people take or how well workers are matched to their job
    • Taxi driver with PhD counts as fully employed
  • Part-time worker who wants full-time job still counts as fully employed
  • There is a difference between productive labor and unproductive labor
    • Institutions like property, prices, and profit/loss incentives guide labor to where it is most highly valued
    • Government can create jobs that are worse than useless—they use scarce resources and create nothing of value
ECON 104
12

Types of Unemployment

ECON 104
13

1. Frictional Unemployment

Frictional unemployment is short-term unemployment caused by the difficulty of matching employee to employer.

  • This is the labor market analogue of clothes sitting on the shelves at Target.
  • Everyone wants to buy at a low enough price—but nobody wants to sell.
  • Finding a price that the buyer (the firm) is willing to pay and the seller (the laborer) is willing to accept takes time.
  • Comes down to costly information
    • Employees don’t know about all possible job opportunities
    • Employers don’t know about all possible job candidates
ECON 104
14

Frictional Unemployment

  • This is usually a large share of total US unemployment
  • US economy is dynamic – meaning millions of jobs are created and destroyed every month

What causes frictional unemployment?

  1. The time it takes for employers and employees to find each other
  2. New workers entering the workforce (after graduating college, perhaps)
  3. Workers looking for work after changing careers
  4. Employees leaving old jobs to find new jobs better suited to their skills
ECON 104
18

It may be a sign of a healthy economy!!

  • To get rid of frictional unemployment, force every worker to accept the first job they’re offered no matter the wage.
  • Would this be good for the economy?
  • The economy restructures itself in response to changing circumstances, consumer demands, technological innovations, and resource availability.
ECON 104
19

2. Structural Unemployment

Structural unemployment is persistent, long-term unemployment.

  • “Long-term” meaning that a substantial portion of the unemployed have been unemployed for more than a year
  • “Persistent” meaning that this has been the case for a long time
  • In France, Germany, Italy, and Spain, approximately 40% to 50% of the unemployed have been unemployed for more than a year, and this has been true for about 25 years
ECON 104
20

What causes structural unemployment?

  1. Mismatch between the skills employees have and the skills employers want
    1. Even if there are new jobs available, workers can’t get them without retraining
    2. Shift from manufacturing to service economy
  2. Major, economy-wide changes in technology
    1. Economy takes a while to restructure in response to these shocks
ECON 104
21

Structural Unemployment

  • But over time, technological innovations lead to lower costs, increased production, and overall improvements in living standards as the economy adjusts to shocks, moving workers to where their labor is more highly valued.
  • However, despite rising average living standards, certain workers can get left behind in an unemployment trap.
  • Think about parents who want to rejoin the labor force after a break – they may find it more difficult because their skills might not be matched for the current technology.
ECON 104
22

Structural Unemployment and labor market regulations

Unemployment benefits
  • This increases unemployment by lowering the cost of remaining unemployed
  • In Europe, unemployment benefits are higher and last longer
  • Lower incentive for unemployed to search for jobs
  • Unsurprisingly, the unemployment rate is higher in Europe
ECON 104
23

Structural Unemployment and labor market regulations

Minimum wage
  • At the minimum wage, supply exceeds demand, leading to a surplus of labor that we call unemployment.
  • The same effect occurs for unions raising the wage rate
ECON 104
24

Minimum wage and union wages

Minimum wage
Union wage
ECON 104
25

Structural Unemployment and labor market regulations

Hiring and firing costs
  • Around the world, it is not uncommon for the government to impose restrictions on firing and hiring by firms.
  • In Portugal, a firm needs to get the government’s permission to lay off a group of workers.
  • In India, if you’re a firm with more than 500 workers, you need the permission of the government to lay someone off.
  • If it is costly for you to fire (incompetent) workers, you are less likely to also hire them.
  • This increases the cost to the firm of hiring and firing workers, making firms slow to adjust to changing circumstances and leading to long-term unemployment

3. Cyclical Unemployment

Cyclical unemployment is unemployment correlated with the ups and downs of the business cycle.

  • During recessions, unemployment increases dramatically
  • When GDP is falling, firms tend to lay off workers
  • High unemployment means there is lots of idle labor, which implies lots of idle capital, which implies lower economic growth
  • Unemployment is higher when real GDP growth is below average and lower when it is above average
ECON 104
28

Cyclical Unemployment

Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics via FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (UNRATE). Shaded areas indicate U.S. recessions. Retrieved October 5, 2026.
ECON 104
29

Cyclical Unemployment

  • Some economists think that cyclical unemployment is the result of wages being out of synch with the price level.
  • In plain English, the price level is too low and the wage rate is too high.
  • When prices are low and wages are high, this means it is unprofitable for firms to hire more workers.
  • The general idea is that while prices for products rise and fall sharply, wages are “sticky.”
ECON 104
30

Natural Unemployment Rate

  1. Frictional + structural unemployment
  2. True unemployment varies around this natural rate
  3. These change slowly over time
  4. Things like internet job applications may lower the frictional unemployment rate, causing the natural unemployment rate to fall

What affects the LFPR?

  1. Lifecycle effects and demographics
  2. Incentives (wages)
  3. Technology
  4. Cultural Changes
  5. Changes in tastes and domestic production

Claudia Goldin: married women in work

Figure: Johan Jarnestad / The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, popular science background to the 2023 Prize in Economic Sciences.
ECON 104
36

Claudia Goldin: the U-shaped curve

  • Women’s participation does not simply rise with economic growth.
  • Over two centuries it traces a U: it fell as the economy industrialized, then rose again with the growth of the service sector.
  • Women’s work was undercounted in the records. Corrected for this, the employment rate of married women around 1900 was almost three times what the census showed.
ECON 104
37

Claudia Goldin: what held women back, and what changed it

Marriage bars
  • Rules that kept married women out of jobs like teaching and office work, strongest in the 1930s
Expectations
  • Young women in the 1950s did not expect long careers, so they chose their education accordingly
The pill
  • From the late 1960s, women could plan: they delayed marriage and childbirth and studied more economics, law, and medicine
